1.x: “out of the house”: this signifies a shift from private or semi-private instruction to a public address. “The house” probably refers to his base of operations in Capernaum (often associated with Peter’s house).

2.x: Jesus sits on a ship in the Sea of Galilee.

3.x: These verses set the stage for the “Parabolic Discourse” (Mt 13:3-52). Jesus begins to teach exclusively in parables to the crowds, using “veiled language” that required spiritual discernment to understand, thus distinguishing between those who were merely curious observers and those who were true, receptive disciples.

4.x: Jesus begins with the Parable of the Sower. This is the first of seven parables in this discourse. Jesus describes 4 distinct environments where the seed (the message) is dropped. In the context of 1st-century Galilee, farmers often sowed seed before plowing, meaning the seed would land on various types of ground: (1) By the Way Side: The hard-packed footpath running through or alongside the field - seed cannot penetrate; birds eat it immediately.

7.x: (3) Among Thorns: Soil that looks good but contains the seeds/roots of weeds and briers - the thorns grow faster and taller, “choking” the plants by stealing sunlight and nutrients.

8.x: (4) Good Ground: Deep, clean, nutrient-rich soil - produces a crop far exceeding the standard harvest, yielding 30, 60, or 100 times what was sown. A typical good harvest in that region was often closer to 7:1 or 10:1. 30:1, 60:1 & 100:1 emphasize the supernatural power of the “seed” when it finds the right environment.

9.x: “This is a call to active discernment. It signals that the literal story of farming contains a deeper, spiritual reality that requires more than just physical hearing to grasp. Jesus was illustrating the various responses he was currently receiving from his audience. Some (like the Pharisees) were “hard soil,” while others were “shallow” or “distracted.” This parable acts as a diagnostic tool for the listener to examine their own receptivity to his teaching.

10.x: The disciples recognize that Jesus’ method has changed.

11.x: “Mysteries of the kingdom”: a divine truth that was previously hidden but has now been revealed by God. “it is given unto you.. but to them it is not given”: predestination is not the context here; this is about PRESENT receptivity to Jesus’ teaching and judicial hardening in response to unbelief; this IS NOT about an eternal decree of predestination about who can or cannot believe. Jesus’ response implies a distinction between two groups: (1) The Disciples: Those who have committed to following Jesus and have the “eyes to see & ears to hear.” For them the parables are a gateway that leads to deeper understanding. (2) The Outsides (The Crowds/Religious leaders): Those who have rejected or remain indifferent to Jesus’ message. For them, the parables function as a form of judicial hardening. Because they have rejected the plain truth, the message is now given to them in a form that will not be digested by simply passively listening by. Jesus “is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Heb 11:6 KJV); only those who thirst for knowledge & wisdom would make the effort to get to know more about Jesus:. “If thou seekest her(wisdom) as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures” (Prov 2:4 KJV), then the LORD will provide wisdom, knowledge, and understanding (Prov 2:6). He wants to be found, but he also wants to be searched for. This is not predestination because: (1) The context is the people’s response to Jesus’ teaching. Right after v.11 Jesus explains WHY he speaks in parables: “Because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.” (v.13). Then he quotes Isaiah 6: “For this people’s heart is waxed gross, and their ears are dull of hearing, and their eyes they have closed…” (v.15). Notice the wording: “THEY HAVE CLOSED” their eyes. The blindness is not described as God arbitrarily closing their eyes before birth. It is presented as their own persistent response to the revelation they were receiving. (2) “Given” does not mean “eternally predetermined”. “Unto you it is given..” In Matthew, “given” often means GRANTED or PERMITTED by God in a moment, not necessarily decreed before creation. Examples: “flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee…” (Mt 16:17 KJV) - Peter receives revelation. “All men cannot receive this saying, save they to whom it is given.” (Mt 19:11 KJV) - this doesn’t imply eternal predestination; it means capacity is granted by God. So Mt 13:11 can simply mean: “God has granted the disciples understanding at this time” not “God eternally decreed everyone else can never understand.” (3) The disciples themselves were not naturally understanding. Throughout Matthew they often misunderstand Jesus: they fear in the storm,misunderstand leaven, fail to understand predictions of the cross and ask for explanations repeatedly. In Mt 13:36, they literally have to ask: “Explain to us the parable..” (Mt 13:36 BSB). Their understanding is a gift of grace and continued instruction, not proof that they were predestined while everyone else was passed over. (4) Jesus ends repeatedly: “Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.” (v.9). This invitation makes little sense if the point is: “some were eternally created unable to hear.” Instead, the parables also function as a call to respond. (5) Matthew also emphasizes human responsibility, not inability: “how often would I have gathered thy children together… AND YE WOULD NOT!” Not: “and ye could not because you were not predestined.” But: “ye would not.” Likewise Mt 11:20-21, Jesus rebukes cities for not repenting, which assumes genuine responsibility, not predestination. (6) Finally, Isaiah 6 that Jesus quoted shows that Israel had already repeatedly resisted God before the judicial hardening. So the hardening is not arbitrary first-cause predestination. It is a judgement in history upon persistent unbelief & Matthew uses it the same way: Jesus teaches openly, many reject him, hence parables become both revelation to the humble and judgement to the hardened.

Catholics teach that when Jesus says to his disciples: “it is given unto you…but to them it is not given” (v.11), that this refers to Jesus giving revelation to Roman clergy and not to the common people. Their study Bible says: “Jesus’ private instruction of his disciples reflects his intention to arrange the Church hierarchically. He invests his authority in the apostles and their successors to administer the sacraments and transmit God’s truth through their teaching” (Ignatius Catholic Study Bible, Study Notes on Mt 13:11). This is, of course, unbiblical. Apostolic succession is not supported by the Bible, it is an attempt to justify unbiblical teachings within Catholicism. Matthias, the apostle who replaced Judas, was selected as apostle only because he witnessed Jesus in the flesh. In Acts 1:21-22, Peter says that the new apostle must be one of the men who had been with them the whole time the Lord Jesus was living among them, beginning from John’s baptism until Jesus was taken up, so that he could be a witness with them of Jesus’ resurrection. Not a single Roman Clergy has witnessed Jesus in the flesh, hence, the real apostolic authority comes from the very apostolic words written in Scripture. The moment you depart from Scripture is the moment you lose apostolic authority: “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.” (Gal 1:8-9 KJV). This is why, when Paul was about to die (2 Tim 4:6-8), he did not direct Timothy to a human teacher, much less to a Roman clergy. Rather he directed Timothy to Scripture: “And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, WHICH ARE ABLE TO MAKE THEE WISE UNTO SALVATION through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness” (2 Tim 3:15-16 KJV).

12.x: Success breeds success. This verse explains the “dividing line” mentioned in the previous verses. It functions as a spiritual law of cause and effect on a person’s initial response to the truth. “Whosoever hath”: This refers to the person who has receptivity. If a listener has even a small amount of genuine faith, desire for truth, or “good soil" in his heart, God provides the grace and insight to increase that understanding. He “is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Heb 11:6 KJV). The result is an “abundance” of spiritual clarity. “Whosoever hath not”: This refers to the person who lacks receptivity or has a hardened heart. It is not that they are naturally “empty,” but rather that they have rejected what was already given to them (natural revelation, the Law, or Jesus’ previous plain teachings). ‘“From him shall be taken away even that he hath”: This is the “judicial” aspect of the teaching. When a person consistently ignores or rejects the truth, they eventually lose the capacity to recognize it at all. Their “spiritual ears” stop functioning, and the light they once had is extinguished by their own indifference or hostility. Whatever understanding they had is eventually lost. Jesus is illustrating that there is no neutral ground, you are either moving toward greater light or sliding into deeper darkness. The pattern is dynamic: “response” → “more light” or “rejection” → “greater blindness” RATHER THAN predestined “elect” → “non-elect.”

13.x: To those who have persistently rejected his message, the parables function as a form of divine judgement. Because they have already chosen to shut their eyes and ears to the plain truth of his earlier ministry, they are now left with stories they cannot (or will not) understand.

33.x: The Parable of the Leaven (or Yeast). Unlike the mustard seed, which illustrates the Kingdom’s external growth, the leaven illustrates its internal transformation. Leaven is a microscopic agent that, once introduced, works silently and invisibly to change the nature of the entire mass of dough. The “leavening” process is irreversible. Once the yeast is “hid” (or “mixed in” from enkrypten - where the word “encryption” comes from - meaning “hidden” or “buried” in the dough), the flour is forever changed; it is no longer just flour, but dough ready to become bread. This represents how the gospel, once introduced into a culture or a life, initiates a fundamental, molecular change in its character. The quantity mentioned: “three measures” (“three sata in Greek, or sixty pounds) is a massive amount of flour, enough to bake bread for a small village or a very large gathering, hence: a tiny, almost imperceptible amount of yeast is sufficient to transform a colossal amount of material.

34.x: “unto the multitude”: the text clarifies that parables was his public method during this season of his ministry. As mentioned earlier, this was in fulfillment of Isaiah’s prophecy, serving both to reveal truth to the prepared and to veil it from those with hardened hearts. Parables was the norm, so much that his disciples would be amazed when he didn’t use them: “now speakest thou plainly, and speakest thou no proverb” (Jn 16:29-30 KJV). The “plain speaking” was reserved for the core group of the disciples. This was the process of forming the administrative and theological foundation of the movement. By speaking plainly, Jesus was transitioning them from being mere listeners to being the foundational stewards of the message.

35.x: Matthew is citing Psalm 78:2. While the verse attributes the quote to “the prophet,” it specifically refers to Asaph the Seer, who was a levitical leader and a composer of psalms. “Things which have been kept secret”: these “secrets” are not magical spells or gnostic riddles. They are the mysteries of the Kingdom - specifically the idea that God’s reign would arrive in a humble, gradual, and inclusive way, rather than through a sudden military conquest. By saying these truths were hidden “from the foundation of the world,” Jesus is saying that the Plan of Redemption was not a “Plan B.” It was a pre-ordained, structural reality of the universe that remained veiled until the person of Jesus arrived to “un-hide” it. The Crucifixion of the Son WAS THE ORIGINAL PLAN even before anything was created. God was not going to create a World without a way to save it. “Who verily was FOREORDAINED before the foundation of the world” (1 Pet 1:19-20 KJV); “according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus BEFORE THE WORLD BEGAN” (2 Tim 1:9 KJV); “O Father, glorify thou me with thine own self with THE GLORY WHICH I HAD WITH THEE BEFORE THE WORLD WAS” (Jn 17:5 KJV) (remember Jesus was “glorified” at Cavalry: Jn 12:23-24); “whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb SLAIN FROM THE FOUNDATION OF THE WORLD” (Rev 13:8 KJV). John 1 also speaks of this foreordained plan of God: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. The same was in the beginning with God. All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.” (Jn 1:1-3 KJV). Many Trinitarians wrongly assume that there are two persons who are God in here by literally changing the definition of “God” mid-sentence. This is how they read it: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with [God-the-Father], and the Word was [God-the-Son]”. This is an academic dishonest reading of the verse, not just for changing the definition of “God” mid-sentence, but also for changing the definition of the “Word” (Logos). John wrote in Greek for a Greek audience. In Greek thought, the Logos WAS NEVER A PERSON, rather it was the rationale, the plan, the order of the Universe. So, if we read John 1 within its 1st-century context: “In the beginning was the Word(wisdom/plan/command/rationale)”: Before creation, God had a plan for redemption. “The Word(wisdom/plan/command/rationale) was WITH God”: The plan resided within God’s own mind and purpose. “The Word(wisdom/plan/command/rationale) WAS God”: The plan was not a separate entity; wisdom is the very essence of YHWH. God, being outside of time, saw the fall of man before He even spoke “Let there be light.” The Logos is the “blueprint” of the Incarnation. God didn’t “become” a Father in eternity (Heb 1:5); He held the concept of the Son (the humanity) within His Word. The Logos is the SPOKEN DECREE OF REDEMPTION. God’s speech is creative; when He “speaks” a plan, it is as good as done. “All things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made.” (Jn 1:3 KJV) - a poetic way of saying that everything was created with the sacrifice of the Son in mind. Then, “when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth(as God “sent” John the Baptist as well) His Son, MADE(begotten) of a woman, MADE under the law” (Gal 4:4 KJV). “Thou art my Son, THIS DAY(not eternally back) have I begotten thee(in Mary under the Law)” And again, I WILL(future tense) be to him a Father, and HE SHALL(future tense) be to me a Son” (Heb 1:5 KJV). This pivots to: “And the Word(the one God who is Spirit) was made flesh, and DWELT(the Greek means “tabernacled”) among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth” (Jn 1:14 KJV). In the human Jesus “dwelleth the fullness of the Godhead bodily(the Word)” (Col 2:9 KJV); “God was IN Christ, reconciling the world unto Himself” (2 Cor 5:19 KJV) - the one YHWH, our redeemer, came to reconcile us to Himself in Jesus. It is in this way that the “Word was made flesh,” the Plan became a Person. The eternal Spirit (the Father) took on a human nature (the Son). Jesus is not “God the Son” (an eternal person), but the “Son of God” - God manifest in the flesh. The Logos (that original thought of redemption) was “clothed” in humanity. Therefore, when you look at Jesus, you aren’t looking at a “second person” of a Trinity; you are looking at the visible image of the invisible YHWH (Col 1:15). “Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Show us the Father?” (Jn 14:9 KJV). The Word of Jesus is the Word of the Father speaking through Him: “For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” (Jn 12:49 KJV).

44.x: The Parable of the Hidden Treasure. In the 1st century Near East, in an era without modern banking systems, burying valuables in the ground was a common way to protect them from invading armies or bandits. If the owner died without revealing the location, the treasure remained hidden until someone stumbled upon it. Under Rabbinic law at the time, if a person found lost money or a vessel and could not identify the owner, it belonged to the finder. By buying the field, the man ensures legal ownership of everything within its boundaries, securing his right to the treasure. The parable shows that the man “sells all that he has.” This emphasizes that while the Kingdom is a “find” (often appearing as a gift or a surprise), entering into it requires a total realignment of one’s priorities. The primary point is the surpassing worth of the Kingdom. The “treasure” is so valuable that any sacrifice made to obtain it is not actually a sacrifice at all, but a logical and profitable exchange. Note that the man doesn’t sell his possessions out of a sense of grim duty or legalistic obligation. He does it “for joy thereof.” This suggests that following Christ is not a burdensome loss of one’s life, but a joyful trade of something temporary for something eternal. Also, unlike the merchant in the next parable who is actively seeking pearls, this man seems to stumble upon the treasure. This shows that for many, the realization of the gospel comes as a divine calling: a sudden, life-changing interruption to their daily routine. This also serves as a counterpoint to the earlier “tares” and “hard soil.” While many reject the message or allow it to be choked by thorns, the person described here recognizes the true value of what Jesus is offering.

49.x: Jesus explains the “hauling in” of the net as a representation of the end of time. The angels are the ones who come forth to “sever the wicked from among the just,” showing again that the final judgement is a divine prerogative, not a human one.

50.x: Jesus repeats the somber warning of “wailing and gnashing of teeth.” In context, this is a call to realize that being “in the net” (associating with the Kingdom or the church) is not the same as being “good” (truly transformed by the Kingdom). The net gathers “some of every king,” showing the global reach of the gospel message. It touches everyone, but not everyone responds by becoming “good fish.” And just as the wheat and tares grew together, the “good” and the “bad” fish remain in the same net until the very end. This parable warns against complacency. Being caught in the “gospel net” (hearing the word) is only the beginning; the final evaluation depends on whether one has actually been made righteous by the “seed” of the Word.

57.x: This verse shows how internal bias and “familiarity” can act as a literal barrier to experiencing divine power. The Greek word used for “offended” is skandalizō, from which the English word “scandalize” comes from. In the original context, a skandalon was the trigger-stick of a trap or a stumbling block in a path. The people of Nazareth didn’t just “disagree” with Jesus; they “tripped” over him. His ordinary background (the carpenter’s son) became a hurdle they couldn’t get over to see his messianic identity. “A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country”: Familiarity breeds contempt. When a community has seen someone grow up, lose their baby teeth, and work a common trade, they struggle to accept that person as a vessel for the voice of God. To the people of Nazareth, Jesus was “Jesus the neighbor”, which prevented them from seeing him as “Jesus the Lord.”

58.x: This does not mean that Jesus “lost his power” or that his ability was dependent on human permission. Rather, it speaks to the purpose of his miracles. Jesus’ miracles were never mere “magic shows” to entertain the curious; they were signs intended to confirm the message of the Kingdom to those with “ears to hear.” In an atmosphere of systemic rejection and cynicism, performing miracles would have been “throwing pearls before swine” (Mt 7:6). God rarely forces His presence where He is explicitly rejected. Because the “soil” of Nazareth was hard and unreceptive, the “seed” of His power was not sown there in abundance.

5-6.x: (2) Stony Places: Plants sprout quickly due to the warmth of the rock, but wither because they have no depth for moisture.

14-15.x: Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 to explain this phenomenon. It describes a spiritual reality: when people repeatedly ignore the truth, they gradually lose the capacity to perceive it. Their hearts have “grown callous,”(BSB) making them morally and spiritually incapable of “turning” (repenting) toward God. It is possible to hear the Word of God constantly yet fail to grasp its life-transforming significance.

16-17.x: “Many prophets and righteous men have desired to see”: This highlights that the arrival of the Kingdom in the person of Jesus is the culmination of everything the prophets of old had anticipated. The disciples are witnessing the “mystery” revealed - the very thing the faithful of Israel had waited centuries to behold. Jesus’ teaching suggests that those who have been given insight are responsible for acting upon it. The “blessing” of seeing and hearing is meant to lead to obedience and fruitfulness.

18-23.x: Jesus explains the Parable of the Sower in plain language. In every scenario, the message (the “word of the kingdom”) is exactly the same. The failure of the crop is never blamed on the quality of the seed or the skill of the sower. The only factor that distinguishes the “good soil” from the others is fruitfulness. In Jesus’ teaching, the evidence of true hearing is a changed life that eventually produces a spiritual harvest. These are described as the Fruits of the Spirit: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.” (Gal 5:22-23 KJV). “He that soweth, soweth to the heart” (Study Note on Mt 13:19 from the Geneva Bible).

24-30.x: Jesus presents the Parable of the Tares (or Weeds). The narrative plot goes like: (1) A man sows good seed in his field; (2) While everyone is sleeping, an enemy comes and sows “tares” (or weeds, from the Greek “zizania”, which is poisonous grass that looks almost identical to wheat until it matures) among the wheat. (3) When the crops sprout, the servants notice the tares. They ask the master, “Do you want us to pull them up?” (4) The Master: “No, because while you are pulling the tares, you may uproot the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest.” Jesus acknowledges that the Kingdom of God exists in a world that is not yet fully redeemed. The presence of “tares” (evil, falsehood, or those who oppose God) alongside the “wheat” (the followers of Christ) is an inevitable reality of the present age. By choosing a plant that is nearly indistinguishable from wheat during its early growth, Jesus highlights that evil often masquerades as good. It is often only at the “harvest” (the end of age) that the true nature of what has been sown becomes fully apparent. The master’s command to wait is a profound statement on divine grace and timing. The servants’ desire to “clean the field” is an impulsive human reaction - a desire for immediate judgement. However, the master emphasizes that premature intervention would damage the delicate life of the wheat. God’s patience provides space for growth and maturity, even in a compromised environment.

Many Protestant denominations, such as some Presbyterians and Reformed Baptists (those who adhere to pre-destination) teach that the millennial kingdom happens before Chirst’s second coming. This is often labeled: Postmillennialism (Jesus returns post-millennial). They teach that the gospel will increasingly transform the world, making things better & leading to a more righteous age(the millennium); then Christ will return after that period to consummate his kingdom. However, the Parable of the Tares seems to contradict that. It suggests that the Church or community should not expect a purified environment before the end. As the rest of Scripture also strongly suggests: “This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy...” (2 Tim 3:1-5 KJV); “But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived.” (2 Tim 3:13 KJV); “And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.” (Mt 24:12 KJV); “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith...” (1 Tim 4:1 KJV); etc. Movements like Christian Nationalism (which aim to establish God’s Kingdom on Earth to prepare the world for the Messiah), will not work because “against [the Fruits of the Spirit] there is no law” (Gal 5:22-23 KJV). You cannot force obedience in people. History teaches us this in the atrocities committed by the “Christian” Roman Empire. The responsibility of the believer is not to act as the ultimate judge of others (which would lead to many uprooting “wheat” rather than actual “tares”), but to remain faithful and productive (“wheat”) until the harvest. The final sorting is reserved for God at the end of the age, ensuring perfect justice.

31-32.x: The Parable of the Mustard Seed. The mustard seed was often used in rabbinic tradition as an idiom for the smallest possible object. Jesus uses this to emphasize that the Kingdom of God does not arrive with the political or military grandeur that many in 1st-century Israel expected. It begins with a seemingly insignificant, humble start. While the seed is small, it contains the “DNA” of a mature tree. This highlights that the Kingdom operates according to an internal, divine vitality. It does not rely on external force or mass coercion to grow; it grows from within. The transformation from a tiny seed to a large tree is presented as an inevitable biological process of the power of the gospel. “The birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof”: The branches could refer to the multiple denominations within Christianity that truthfully worship God and accurately proclaim the gospel of “rest” to people, or it could be using allusions to the OT (specifically Eze 17:23 & Dan 4:12), in which birds find rest in tree branches that represent the nations of the world, which provide refuge and shelter to God’s people. If the latter, this signaled that the Kingdom would eventually extend beyond Israel to provide sanctuary for all.

36-43.x: Jesus provides a private decoding of the Parable of the Tares. Just as he did with the Parable of the Sower, he moves away from the crowds and into a house, where he explains the spiritual reality behind the agricultural imagery. Unlike Catholic interpretation that the “field” is the “Church”, Jesus explicitly defines it as “the world.” This suggests that followers of Christ are meant to coexist in the world with those who oppose it until the final judgement. The Greek work of “tares” is “zizania,” likely referring to darnel, a weed that looks almost identical to wheat in its early stages. This detail is crucial: it explains why the servants weren’t allowed to pull the weeds early. Only at the harvest (when the fruit appears) does the distinction become undeniable. Jesus clarifies that the final separation is a divine act, not a human one. The task of judging and “gathering out” belongs to the angels at the “end of age.” For the disciples, this teaching was an exercise in patience. It answered the question of why evil is permitted to persist in a world where the Messiah has already arrived. Jesus explains that the kingdom operates through growth and maturity rather than immediate, violent eradication of opposition.

Roman Catholicism teaches that the field is the “Church”, even though Jesus explicitly says it’s “the world.” (v.38). For Catholicism the wheat represents the true believers, and the tares symbolize false professors or heretics mixed in until final judgement. Hence, the Kingdom of God is the visible Church in which both good and evil coexist. This explains real world Church impurity, and since Jesus forbids early uprooting to prevent damaging true believers (v 29); this parallels Church discipline limits, as full purging risks innocents and awaits Christ’s final harvest. This has long been used to defend the clearly visible imperfections of the Roman Church. However, the parable teaches that believers cannot remove all evil people from the world before the final judgement. It is not forbidding the church from disciplining open sin within the body of believers. In fact, many passages command church discipline. In Matthew 18:15-17, Jesus gives a process of: (1) private rebuke; (2) bring witnesses; (3) tell it to the church; (4) if unrepentant, treat them “ as a heathen man and a publican”. This is explicitly congregational discipline. Paul also commands Christians to remove wicked persons from the church: “Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?” (1 Cor 5:6 KJV); “put away from among yourselves that wicked person” (v.13). He DISTINGUISHES between judging the world versus those inside the church: “For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within?” (v.12). Hence, we do not uproot evil from the world, but the church must deal with open, unrepentant sin inside the church.

45-46.x: Parable of the Pearl of Great Price. In the 1st-century Roman world, pearls were considered the ultimate luxury item, often more valuable than gold. They were sourced from the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf, and the Indian Ocean. Unlike gold, which could be divided, a large, flawless pearl was a single, indivisible unit of wealth. While the result is the same (selling everything), the process of finding the Kingdom differs. The man in the field (v.44) stumbled upon his treasure. This merchant, however, is actively seeking. This represents those who are on a deliberate quest for truth, beauty, or meaning before they finally find Christ, who “he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him” (Heb 11:6 KJV); because "The LORD looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, and seek God." (Ps 14:2 KJV). The merchant was looking for “beautiful pearls” (plural). But once he saw the “one pearl of great price,” he realized his entire collection was secondary. It shows the move from religion (many good deeds or rituals) to the Kingdom (one singular relationship). The pearl presents the absolute unity and sufficiency of the Kingdom. You cannot have a “half a pearl.” You either possess the whole thing or you don’t. And like the previous parable, the merchant sells “all that he had.” Jesus is making the point that the Kingdom is “free” in terms of grace, but it “costs” us our autonomy. We don’t buy the Kingdom with money, but we “buy” it by surrendering our previous life and priorities. This parable also shows that for those who have spent their lives looking for what is “true” and “beautiful,” the gospel is the ultimate answer that renders all other pursuits obsolete.

47-48.x: The Parable of the Net. This was a massive net, often hundreds of feet long, with floats on top and weights on the bottom. It was pulled between two boats or from the shore to the sea and back. Unlike a small hand-cast net, this net was indiscriminate, it swept up everything in its path: fish, seaweed, debris, and “unclean” creatures. Once the next was “full” and hauled to the beach, the fishermen began the arduous task of separation. In Jewish context, this meant separating fish with scales and fins (kosher/edible) from those without (non-kosher/unclean), such as eels or catfish.

51-52.x: Jesus ends the session by asking the disciples if they had understood. He gives one final image about scribes instructed in the kingdom of heaven, and how they become experts in this “new” Kingdom teaching without discarding the “old” (the OT). Instead, they are like a wealthy homeowner who can draw from a vast treasury of both ancient wisdom and fresh revelation to feed others.

53-54.x: Jesus was done and departed into “his own country,” which was Nazareth, the small, obscure village where Jesus grew up. In the 1st-century Jewish context, your “country” or “hometown” was where your family lineage and social status were firmly fixed. To the people of Nazareth, Jesus was not a Rabbi or a Messiah; He was a local carpenter’s son. They don’t deny Jesus is wise or that he performs “mighty works,” they reject the source. They know his “resume” (his family and his trade), they cannot reconcile his ordinary background with his extraordinary authority. Jesus walks into his own hometown and encounters the very “hard soil” he had just preached about.

55-56.x: The NT was written in Greek, which has a specific word for “cousin” (anepsios, used in Col 4:10 by Paul, who specifically calls James Jesus’ adelphoi in Gal 1:19). The NT also has a specific word for “relative” (syngenis), which Luke uses in Lk 1:36, yet even Luke uses adelphoi to describe Jesus’ siblings in Luke 8:19-21. Likewise, Matthew uses adelphos (brother) and adelphē (sister). While adelphos can occasionally be used metaphorically (just like in English and Spanish), when used in a list of immediate family members (mother, father, sisters), the most natural and primary meaning is a sibling. The logic of the crowd’s argument depends on Jesus being entirely ordinary. Their point is: “We know his dad, we know his mom, and we live next door to his brothers and sisters.” If these were “distant cousins” or “step-siblings” from a previous marriage, the “ordinariness” argument loses some of its punch. The crowd is listing the “nuclear family” to prove Jesus is just another local villager. Also, they could not have been siblings from a previous marriage, as Jesus is specifically called the “firstborn” of Mary (Lk 2:7), and as the firstborn, he is the one who inherits the Davidic Kingdom from Joseph & suggests “later-born” siblings. The reason why Jesus left his mother entrusted to John and not his brothers can be easily explained by: (1) the apostle John was Jesus’ cousin. John’s mother (Salome, wife of Zebedee) was Mary’s sister, making James the Great and John cousins. We see this in parallel passages: Matthew 27:56, the “Mother of Zebedee’s sons” = Salome; Mark 15:40, Salome is explicitly mentioned; & John 19:25, “sister” of Mary = Salome. That’s why John had such a close relationship with Jesus as the “disciple whom Jesus loved.” Entrusting Mary to him created a new, spiritual family unit that was not bound by blood, but by shared faith and love. Jesus was symbolically forming the nucleus of the new community of believers. (2) According to John 7:5: "even His brothers did not believe in Him.” It was only after the resurrection that they became central figures in the early Church (with James, the brother of Jessu, eventually becoming a leader in the Jerusalem church). Since they were not present (most likely still in Nazareth, definitely not at the crucifixion site) and were skeptical of Jesus at the time of the crucifixion, they would not have been in a position (physically or spiritually) to care for Mary.
